Graph Signal Generation via Graph-Aware Diffusion Models

Vimal K B    Sergio Rozada    Antonio G. Marques    Elvin Isufi    and Hadi J. Rad ††thanks: V.˜K˜B, E.˜Isufi and H.˜J.˜Rad are with Delft University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands. S.˜Rozada and A.˜G.˜Marques are with King Juan Carlos University, Madrid, Spain.††thanks: This work was partially supported by the Spanish AEI grant PID2022-136887NB-I00 and PID2025-170000NB-I00, the Community of Madrid via the ELLIS Madrid Unit and grants TEC-2024/COM-89, TU Delft AI Labs programme, NWO OTP GraSPA proposal #19497, NWO VENI proposal 222.032, the TU Delft - Shell.ai TKI project, and by the SURE-AI Centre grant #357482, Research Council of Norway.
Abstract

Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. They are often partly observed, and learning their distribution enables imputing missing values and forecasting future ones. Diffusion models learn such distributions, but their forward noise is independent across nodes and does not depend on the graph. We introduce graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is a heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise. In the graph Fourier basis, the forward transition is a scalar Gaussian channel at each frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, high graph frequencies are attenuated faster than low ones. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and keeps all of them at the same SNR. For graph-stationary signals, MASS equalizes the normalized error of the optimal linear denoiser across frequencies. We bound reverse-SDE stiffness as a function of the (shifted) Laplacian’s condition number, with a logarithmic upper bound for MASS and a linear lower bound for shared rates. GAD with MASS improves recommendation accuracy by 5–19%, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting MAE and RMSE using only 3 reverse steps.

Index Terms: 
Graph signal generation, graph-aware diffusion, noise scheduling, reverse-time stiffness.

I Introduction

Diffusion models learn a data distribution by gradually corrupting the data with noise and training a neural network, the denoiser, to reverse this corruption [1, 2, 3]. Many signals of interest live on the nodes of a graph [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9], and diffusion models have recently been applied to graph-signal tasks that need plausible samples rather than a single estimate, such as spatio-temporal imputation of traffic readings [10, 11, 12], probabilistic forecasting [13], recommendation from a few user interactions [14, 15], and resource allocation in wireless systems [16, 17]. In these tasks, the observations alone do not determine the signal distribution, and the graph supplies part of the prior by encoding dependencies among nodes.

Most of these models use the graph only in the denoiser or in a conditioning network [10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 18, 19]. Their forward process corrupts every node independently, so their prior is an isotropic Gaussian and the denoiser must learn the interplay between the graph topology and the data, which is costly when data are scarce or the graph is large. Frequency-dependent corruption has been studied mainly for images, either by blurring, which attenuates the high frequencies before the low ones [20, 21, 22], or by setting a different noise variance for each frequency [23, 24]. These methods rely on the Fourier basis of the regular pixel grid, which does not exist on graphs with irregular connections. On any graph, the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian can play the role of Fourier modes and its eigenvalues act as graph frequencies [4]. These provide a direct basis for defining a forward process and its diffusion rates.

We propose graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise [25]. Heat diffusion smooths the signal by attenuating each graph frequency exponentially, the higher frequencies faster. A diffusion rate sets how fast this corruption proceeds. The process has closed-form Gaussian transitions and converges to a Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) defined by the graph Laplacian [26], which we use as the prior. Since this prior already encodes the dependencies between connected nodes, the denoiser does not have to learn them from data, only how the data deviate from them, a task suited to graph filters and graph neural networks [27].

The noise schedule sets the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the corrupted signal at each diffusion time, i.e., the power of the surviving signal relative to that of the added noise. The SNR affects how much of the clean signal the denoiser can recover [28, 29, 30]. In isotropic diffusion, every direction is attenuated equally, and the SNRs differ only through the power spectrum of the data [23]. In GAD, the SNR of each graph frequency depends on its clean power (set by the data), its prior power (set by the graph), and its attenuation, which decays exponentially with the graph frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, the SNRs separate exponentially in the frequency gap as the integrated rate grows. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which sets the diffusion rate of each graph frequency from its clean power and its prior power, so that all graph frequencies share the same SNR at every diffusion time.

A preliminary version of this work [25] introduced the GAD forward process with a shared polynomial diffusion rate (FCPS) and a limited evaluation. This journal version develops the spectral theory of the process, introduces frequency-dependent diffusion rates with guarantees on denoising error and reverse-SDE stiffness, and substantially broadens the evaluation. Our contributions are as follows.

  • C1

    Spectral analysis of GAD (Sections III and IV). GAD has a scalar Gaussian forward channel with closed-form SNR at each graph frequency. Under graph stationarity, we characterize the optimal linear denoising error and the fixed-time training rate at each graph frequency.

  • C2

    Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (Section V). MASS gives each graph frequency its own diffusion rate so that all share the same SNR, without changing the GMRF prior. Under graph stationarity, the optimal linear denoiser then has the same normalized error at every graph frequency. The stiffness of the reverse SDE admits a logarithmic upper bound with MASS and a linear lower bound with a shared rate, in terms of the condition number of the shifted Laplacian.

  • C3

    Empirical validation (Section VI). On synthetic graph signals, MASS reduces the stiffness diagnostic for the diffusion rate by factors of 4.88×1024.88{\times}10^{2} to 1.49×1051.49{\times}10^{5} and improves sample quality at a fixed number of reverse steps. On downstream tasks, it improves recommendation metrics by 55–19%19\%, reduces imputation RMSE by up to 7.8%7.8\% with half the reverse steps, and lowers forecasting MAE and RMSE with only 33 reverse steps.11 1 The code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/vimalkb7/SpectralAnalysisGAD.

II Context and Background

II-A Related Work

We review prior work on the forward process, the noise schedule, and the sampler. Most existing diffusion models for graph signals use isotropic forward noise, and the graph is used only by the denoiser or the conditioning variables [10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 18, 17, 31].

Structured forward processes either shape the noise covariance or make the drift graph-aware [32]. In the first case, the covariance is fixed in advance, built from the data domain, or estimated from the conditioning signal [33, 34, 35, 36, 37], but the drift does not propagate the signal along the edges, and the terminal covariance is chosen rather than reached as the invariant law of the dynamics. In the second case, the forward process blurs images [20, 21] or filters signals over a graph [38, 39, 40, 41, 42], and attenuates each frequency at a rate proportional to its eigenvalue. Under a diffusion rate shared by all frequencies, the SNRs of the high and low frequencies then separate, and the effect of this separation on training and sampling has not been analyzed for generative modeling. GAD belongs to this second group. Its GMRF prior encodes the graph, so the denoiser does not have to learn it, and MASS controls how this prior interacts with the data by setting the diffusion rate of each graph frequency from its clean power and its prior power.

Noise schedules set the SNR of each component of the signal through the shape of the schedule [43], the terminal condition [44], the eigenvalues of a graph [40], or a learned network [28, 45]. In all cases, the SNR of a component is a by-product of these choices, and different components take very different SNRs at the same diffusion time. For linear denoising of a single component, the optimal estimator approximately inverts the attenuation at high SNR and approaches the prior mean at low SNR [46, 47]. Reweighting the denoising error over diffusion time rescales the contribution of each time but leaves the SNR of each component at that time unchanged [46]. MASS instead sets the SNR of every graph frequency directly. Table I summarizes these axes.

Diffusion models also fit different frequency components of the data at different rates [48, 49, 50]. For a spectral linear denoiser, the fixed-time training constant of a component is inversely proportional to its corrupted power. In sampling, all graph frequencies share one integration grid, and stiffness in the reverse drift can restrict the step size of explicit solvers, as for ill-conditioned scores across scales on images [51]. Fast samplers reduce the number of steps without changing the forward process [52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60], and graph-signal models adopt them directly [13, 14, 40]. MASS instead changes the forward process itself, so that all graph frequencies share the same reverse-SDE gain.

II-B Preliminaries

Graph signal processing. Let 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) be an undirected graph on n=|𝒱|n=|\mathcal{V}| nodes, with weighted adjacency matrix 𝐀∈ℝ≥0n×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n\times n}. A graph signal 𝐱∈ℝn\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} assigns the value xix_{i} to node ii. We encode the topology through the Laplacian 𝐋=𝐃−𝐀\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{D}-\mathbf{A}, with degree matrix 𝐃=𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀⁡(𝐀𝟏)\mathbf{D}=\mathsf{diag}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{1}). Since 𝐋\mathbf{L} is symmetric positive semidefinite, it admits the eigendecomposition

𝐋=𝐕​𝚲​𝐕𝖳,𝚲=𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀⁡(λ0=0,…,λn−1),\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\mathbf{\Lambda}=\mathsf{diag}(\lambda_{0}=0,\ldots,\lambda_{n-1}), (1)

with 𝐕=[𝐯0,…,𝐯n−1]\mathbf{V}=[\mathbf{v}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{n-1}] the eigenvectors and 𝚲\mathbf{\Lambda} the respective eigenvalues. The columns of 𝐕\mathbf{V} form an orthonormal graph Fourier basis, with graph Fourier transform (GFT) and inverse GFT 𝐱~=𝐕𝖳​𝐱\mathbf{\tilde{x}}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x} and 𝐱=𝐕​𝐱~\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{\tilde{x}}, respectively [5]. We write x~k=𝐯k𝖳​𝐱\tilde{x}_{k}=\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x} for the kkth GFT coefficient of 𝐱\mathbf{x}. For Laplacians, it holds that 𝐱𝖳​𝐋𝐱=∑(i,j)∈ℰAi,j​(xi−xj)2\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}A_{i,j}(x_{i}-x_{j})^{2} and hence λk=𝐯k𝖳​𝐋𝐯k=∑(i,j)∈ℰAi,j​([𝐯k]i−[𝐯k]j)2\lambda_{k}=\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{v}_{k}=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}A_{i,j}([\mathbf{v}_{k}]_{i}-[\mathbf{v}_{k}]_{j})^{2}. That is, eigenvectors associated with small eigenvalues vary slowly across connected nodes, and their eigenvalues are the low graph frequencies, while eigenvectors associated with large eigenvalues oscillate between neighbors, and their eigenvalues are the high graph frequencies [4]. In turn, the kkth GFT coefficient x~k\tilde{x}_{k} captures the signal contribution along the kkth graph frequency λk\lambda_{k}.

Graph filters. A graph convolutional filter of order KK is a matrix polynomial of 𝐋\mathbf{L} [7],

𝐲=h𝜽​(𝐋)​𝐱,h𝜽​(𝐋)=∑m=0Kθm​𝐋m,\mathbf{y}=h_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{L})\mathbf{x},\qquad h_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{L})=\sum_{m=0}^{K}\theta_{m}\mathbf{L}^{m}, (2)

with coefficients 𝜽=[θ0,…,θK]𝖳\boldsymbol{\theta}=[\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{K}]^{\mathsf{T}}. Since 𝐋m\mathbf{L}^{m} couples mm-hop neighborhoods, (2) propagates the input signal 𝐱\mathbf{x} over the graph with θm\theta_{m} weighting each neighborhood. As 𝐋m=𝐕​𝚲m​𝐕𝖳\mathbf{L}^{m}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{\Lambda}^{m}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}, the filter acts pointwise on graph frequencies,

y~k=h𝜽​(λk)​x~k,h𝜽​(λ)=∑m=0Kθm​λm,\tilde{y}_{k}=h_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\lambda_{k})\,\tilde{x}_{k},\qquad h_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\lambda)=\sum_{m=0}^{K}\theta_{m}\lambda^{m}, (3)

where y~k\tilde{y}_{k} is the kkth GFT coefficient of the output 𝐲\mathbf{y} and h𝜽​(λ)h_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\lambda) is the filter frequency response. More generally, given a scalar function h:ℝ→ℝh:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, a spectral graph filter is the function of the Laplacian,

h⁡(𝐋)=𝐕​𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀​(h⁡(λ0),…,h⁡(λn−1))​𝐕𝖳.h(\mathbf{L})=\mathbf{V}\mathsf{diag}\!\bigl(h(\lambda_{0}),\ldots,h(\lambda_{n-1})\bigr)\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}. (4)

Graph neural networks. A graph neural network (GNN) is defined by the propagation rule at layer ℓ=0,…,NL−1\ell=0,\ldots,N_{L}-1

𝐗(ℓ+1)=ϕ⁡(∑m=0Kℓ𝐋m​𝐗(ℓ)​𝐖m(ℓ)),𝐗(0)=𝐗\mathbf{X}^{(\ell+1)}=\mathsf{\phi}\!\left(\sum_{m=0}^{K_{\ell}}\mathbf{L}^{m}\mathbf{X}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}_{m}^{(\ell)}\right),\quad\mathbf{X}^{(0)}=\mathbf{X} (5)

where 𝐗(ℓ)\mathbf{X}^{(\ell)} collects the node features at layer ℓ\ell, 𝐖m(ℓ)\mathbf{W}_{m}^{(\ell)} are learnable feature-mixing matrices, KℓK_{\ell} is the filter order, and ϕ\mathsf{\phi} is the entrywise nonlinearity. Before the activation, the graph filter bank acts separately on each graph frequency, mixing features through {𝐖m(ℓ)}m\{\mathbf{W}_{m}^{(\ell)}\}_{m}. The nodewise activation can then mix graph frequencies.

Graph heat diffusion. Heat diffusion on a graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} is defined by the Laplacian-based differential equation [61, 62, 63, 64]

d​𝐮td​t=−c​𝐋𝐮t,𝐮0=𝐱,\frac{d\mathbf{u}_{t}}{dt}=-c\,\mathbf{L}\mathbf{u}_{t},\qquad\mathbf{u}_{0}=\mathbf{x}, (6)

where 𝐮t∈ℝn\mathbf{u}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is a time-varying graph signal and c>0c>0 sets the diffusion rate (speed). The solution of (6) reads as

𝐮t=e−c​t​𝐋​𝐱=ψt​(𝐋)​𝐱,ψt​(λ)=e−c​t​λ,\mathbf{u}_{t}=e^{-ct\mathbf{L}}\mathbf{x}=\psi_{t}(\mathbf{L})\mathbf{x},\qquad\psi_{t}(\lambda)=e^{-ct\lambda},

where e−c​t​𝐋e^{-ct\mathbf{L}} is the graph heat kernel [64], i.e., a spectral graph filter (4) that acts on the GFT coefficients as u~t,k=e−c​t​λk​x~k\tilde{u}_{t,k}=e^{-ct\lambda_{k}}\tilde{x}_{k}. The frequency response ψt​(λ)\psi_{t}(\lambda) is a low-pass filter whose bandwidth shrinks with tt. In the steady state, t→∞t\to\infty, we have e−c​t​λk→0e^{-ct\lambda_{k}}\to 0 for every eigenvalue λk>0\lambda_{k}>0 while for the null eigenvalue we have e−c​t​λ0=1e^{-ct\lambda_{0}}=1, so, for a connected graph, the output converges to the average of the input signal, 𝐮t→𝐯0​𝐯0𝖳​𝐱\mathbf{u}_{t}\to\mathbf{v}_{0}\mathbf{v}_{0}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x}.

Score-based generative modeling. Score-based diffusion models define a forward stochastic process that maps the data distribution 𝐱0∼πdata\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{data}} to a tractable prior 𝐱T∼πT\mathbf{x}_{T}\sim\pi_{T} over a horizon [0,T][0,T], and learn a reverse process that maps samples of πT\pi_{T} back to πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}} [1, 3]. In continuous time, the forward stochastic differential equation (SDE) reads as

d​𝐱t=μ⁡(𝐱t,t)​d​t+β⁡(t)​d​𝐰t,d\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mu(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)\,dt+\beta(t)\,d\mathbf{w}_{t}, (7)

where 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is the state at diffusion time tt with density πt\pi_{t}, 𝐰t\mathbf{w}_{t} is a standard Brownian motion, μ\mu is the drift, and β\beta the diffusion coefficient. Under standard assumptions [65], the reverse-time SDE takes the form

d​𝐱t=[μ⁡(𝐱t,t)−β​(t)2​∇𝐱t​log⁡πt​(𝐱t)]​d​t+β⁡(t)​d​𝐰¯t,d\mathbf{x}_{t}=\left[\mu(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)-\beta(t)^{2}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log\pi_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right]dt+\beta(t)\,d\mathbf{\bar{w}}_{t}, (8)

with 𝐰¯t\mathbf{\bar{w}}_{t} a reverse-time Brownian motion. The score ∇𝐱t​log​πt\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log\pi_{t} is unknown and is learned from data, commonly by denoising [66], where a network predicts from 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} the clean signal, the injected noise, or the score itself [2, 3]. Sampling starts from the terminal prior and integrates (8) backwards.

III Graph-Aware Diffusion

In the forward SDE (10), GAD uses the graph heat flow (6) with a shifted Laplacian and adds Brownian noise. To generate graph signals, GAD starts from a Gaussian prior determined by the graph and solves the reverse SDE (15) with a learned score.

III-A Forward and Reverse Processes

GAD drives the heat flow with the shifted Laplacian

𝐋γ=𝐋+γ​𝐈,γ>0,λγ,k=λk+γ,\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}=\mathbf{L}+\gamma\mathbf{I},\qquad\gamma>0,\qquad\lambda_{\gamma,k}=\lambda_{k}+\gamma, (9)

in place of 𝐋\mathbf{L}. The specialized forward SDE reads as

d​𝐱t=−ct​𝐋γ​𝐱t​d​t+2​ct​σ​d​𝐰t,d\mathbf{x}_{t}=-c_{t}\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}\mathbf{x}_{t}\,dt+\sqrt{2c_{t}}\,\sigma\,d\mathbf{w}_{t}, (10)

with diffusion rate ct≥0c_{t}\geq 0 and noise scale σ>0\sigma>0. The diffusion rate is shared by all graph frequencies, and choosing it is the noise schedule of GAD. Relative to (7), the drift is μ⁡(𝐱,t)=−ct​𝐋γ​𝐱\mu(\mathbf{x},t)=-c_{t}\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}\mathbf{x} and the diffusion coefficient is β⁡(t)=2​ct​σ\beta(t)=\sqrt{2c_{t}}\,\sigma. In the graph Fourier basis, the drift of the kkth GFT coefficient is −ct​λγ,k​x~t,k-c_{t}\lambda_{\gamma,k}\tilde{x}_{t,k}. Since the Laplacian matrix has a zero eigenvalue, the contraction is weakest at λ0=0\lambda_{0}=0, where the drift is −ct​γ​x~t,0-c_{t}\gamma\,\tilde{x}_{t,0}. Without the shift term γ​𝐈\gamma\mathbf{I}, the component associated with the zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian evolves as a time-changed Brownian motion. Its noise variance 2​σ2​c¯t2\sigma^{2}\bar{c}_{t} grows linearly with the integrated rate defined next, precluding a stationary law for (10). Next, we define the integrated rate

c¯t=∫0tcs​𝑑s,c¯0=0,\bar{c}_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}c_{s}\,ds,\qquad\bar{c}_{0}=0, (11)

which we take strictly increasing, with ct>0c_{t}>0 for t>0t>0. Since the drift is linear and the noise additive, the transition of (10) is Gaussian [67],

𝐱t|𝐱0∼𝒩⁡(𝐇t​𝐱0,𝚺t),𝐇t=exp(−c¯t𝐋γ),𝚺t=σ2(𝐈−𝐇t2)𝐋γ−1.\begin{gathered}\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{H}_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}\right),\\[2.0pt] \mathbf{H}_{t}=\exp\!\left(-\bar{c}_{t}\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}\right),\qquad\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}=\sigma^{2}\left(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_{t}^{2}\right)\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}^{-1}.\end{gathered} (12)

Equivalently, the corrupted signal is 𝐱t=𝐇t​𝐱0+𝐞t\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{H}_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\mathbf{e}_{t}, where 𝐞t∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝚺t)\mathbf{e}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}), the attenuation operator 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t} attenuates the clean signal, and 𝐞t\mathbf{e}_{t} is the accumulated forward noise. As the integrated rate grows without bound, c¯t→∞\bar{c}_{t}\to\infty, the attenuation operator vanishes, 𝐇t→𝟎\mathbf{H}_{t}\to\mathbf{0}, and the covariance converges to 𝚺t→σ2​𝐋γ−1\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}\to\sigma^{2}\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}^{-1}. Thus, the limiting distribution is

𝐱∞∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,σ2​𝐋γ−1),\mathbf{x}_{\infty}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{0},\,\sigma^{2}\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}^{-1}\right), (13)

which is a Laplacian-based Gaussian Markov random field. We refer to it as the GMRF prior. At a finite horizon TT, the attenuation operator 𝐇T\mathbf{H}_{T} maps the clean signal to the conditional mean, 𝔼⁡[𝐱T∣𝐱0]=𝐇T​𝐱0\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{T}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}]=\mathbf{H}_{T}\mathbf{x}_{0}. Its squared operator norm, ‖𝐇T‖22=e−2​γ​c¯T\|\mathbf{H}_{T}\|_{2}^{2}=e^{-2\gamma\bar{c}_{T}}, is the worst-case squared attenuation of 𝐇T\mathbf{H}_{T}, determined by the slowest-decaying GFT coefficient, associated with the smallest Laplacian eigenvalue, λ0=0\lambda_{0}=0.

Definition 1 (δ\delta-complete horizon).

For a tolerance δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), the horizon TT is δ\delta-complete if the forward mean retains at most a fraction δ\delta of the clean-signal power at any graph frequency

‖𝐇T‖22=e−2​γ​c¯T≤δ⇔c¯T≥log⁡(1/δ)2​γ.\|\mathbf{H}_{T}\|_{2}^{2}=e^{-2\gamma\bar{c}_{T}}\leq\delta\iff\bar{c}_{T}\geq\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2\gamma}. (14)

The shift γ\gamma sets both the largest prior variance, σ2/γ\sigma^{2}/\gamma, attained at the lowest graph frequency, and the slowest decay of the forward mean, e−γ​c¯te^{-\gamma\bar{c}_{t}}. A smaller γ\gamma therefore preserves more low-frequency variability in the prior but requires a larger integrated rate to reach δ\delta-completeness.

The reverse process requires the score of the marginal density of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, 𝗌t​(𝐱)=∇𝐱​log​πt​(𝐱)\mathsf{s}_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log\pi_{t}(\mathbf{x}). Substituting the drift and the diffusion coefficient of (10) into (8) gives the reverse-time SDE

d​𝐱t=[−ct​𝐋γ​𝐱t−2​ct​σ2​𝗌t​(𝐱t)]​d​t+2​ct​σ​d​𝐰¯t,d\mathbf{x}_{t}=\left[-c_{t}\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}\mathbf{x}_{t}-2c_{t}\sigma^{2}\mathsf{s}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right]dt+\sqrt{2c_{t}}\,\sigma\,d\mathbf{\bar{w}}_{t}, (15)

with 𝐰¯t\mathbf{\bar{w}}_{t} the reverse-time Brownian motion of (8). The score of the transition density is linear in the corrupted signal, ∇𝐱t​log​π​(𝐱t∣𝐱0)=−𝚺t−1​(𝐱t−𝐇t​𝐱0)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log\pi(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})=-\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{H}_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0}), and the score of the marginal is its conditional expectation given 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}. Taking that expectation yields Tweedie’s formula [68],

𝗌t(𝐱t)=−𝚺t−1(𝐱t−𝐇t𝔼[𝐱0∣𝐱t,t]),\mathsf{s}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=-\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{H}_{t}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t]\right), (16)

which expresses the score through the posterior mean of the clean graph signal. GAD estimates that posterior mean by a graph-aware denoising regression. More specifically, let fΘ​(𝐱t,𝐋,t)f_{\Theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{L},t) be a denoiser with parameters Θ\Theta, and let πtr\pi_{\mathrm{tr}} be the uniform distribution on the horizon [0,T][0,T]. Training minimizes the denoising error, i.e., the mean squared error between the clean signal and the denoiser output, over diffusion time and pairs (𝐱0,𝐱t)(\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{x}_{t}) that the forward process generates at that time,

ℒden​(Θ)=𝔼t∼πtr​[𝔼𝐱0∼πdata𝐱t∼π(⋅∣𝐱0,t)​[‖𝐱0−fΘ​(𝐱t,𝐋,t)‖22]],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{den}}(\Theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\pi_{\mathrm{tr}}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{data}}\\ \mathbf{x}_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{0},t)\end{subarray}}\!\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}_{0}-f_{\Theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{L},t)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]\right], (17)

where πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}} is the data distribution and π(⋅∣𝐱0,t)\pi(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{0},t) the transition (12). At each fixed time tt, the posterior mean 𝔼[𝐱0∣𝐱t,t]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t] minimizes the conditional denoising risk in (17) over all square-integrable functions of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}. Denoising is therefore a minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimation problem, and the error of the posterior mean is the MMSE. Substituting the trained denoiser fΘ⋆f_{\Theta^{\star}} for that posterior mean in (16) gives the plug-in score, and with it the learned reverse process (15).

III-B Spectral Characterization

Since the attenuation operator 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t} and covariance 𝚺t\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t} are functions of 𝐋γ\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}, the forward transition, the linear part of the reverse drift, and the coefficients of Tweedie’s formula share its eigenbasis. Expressing the dynamics in this basis gives one equation per graph frequency and makes explicit, for each GFT coefficient, the interplay between its graph frequency, the spectral content of the data, and the shared diffusion rate.

Forward. Let the GFTs of the corrupted signal, the clean signal and the forward noise be 𝐱~t=𝐕𝖳​𝐱t\mathbf{\tilde{x}}_{t}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x}_{t}, 𝐱~0=𝐕𝖳​𝐱0\mathbf{\tilde{x}}_{0}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x}_{0} and 𝐞~t=𝐕𝖳​𝐞t\mathbf{\tilde{e}}_{t}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e}_{t}, with respective kkth coefficients x~t,k\tilde{x}_{t,k}, x~0,k\tilde{x}_{0,k} and e~t,k\tilde{e}_{t,k}. The GFT of the driving noise, 𝐰~t=𝐕𝖳​𝐰t\mathbf{\tilde{w}}_{t}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{w}_{t}, is a standard Brownian motion as 𝐕\mathbf{V} is orthogonal. Using these GFTs, the forward SDE (10) decouples into nn time-inhomogeneous Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equations,

dx~t,k=−ctλγ,kx~t,kdt+2​ctσdw~t,k,k=0,…,n−1.d\tilde{x}_{t,k}=-c_{t}\lambda_{\gamma,k}\tilde{x}_{t,k}\,dt+\sqrt{2c_{t}}\,\sigma\,d\tilde{w}_{t,k},~k=0,...,n-1. (18)

Conditioned on 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}, their solutions are

x~t,k=at,k​x~0,k+e~t,k,e~t,k∼𝒩⁡(0,νt,k),\tilde{x}_{t,k}=a_{t,k}\tilde{x}_{0,k}+\tilde{e}_{t,k},\qquad\tilde{e}_{t,k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\nu_{t,k}), (19)

with attenuation at,ka_{t,k} and noise variance νt,k\nu_{t,k} given by

at,k=exp⁡(−λγ,k​c¯t),νt,k=σ2λγ,k​(1−at,k2).a_{t,k}=\exp\!\left(-\lambda_{\gamma,k}\bar{c}_{t}\right),\qquad\nu_{t,k}=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}\left(1-a_{t,k}^{2}\right). (20)

The attenuation at,ka_{t,k} and the noise variance νt,k\nu_{t,k} are the eigenvalues of 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t} and 𝚺t\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t} on 𝐯k\mathbf{v}_{k}, respectively. The noise coefficients e~t,k\tilde{e}_{t,k} are independent across graph frequencies and independent of 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. The covariance between two distinct corrupted GFT coefficients x~t,j\tilde{x}_{t,j} and x~t,k\tilde{x}_{t,k} equals at,j​at,k​Cov⁡(x~0,j,x~0,k)a_{t,j}a_{t,k}\operatorname{Cov}(\tilde{x}_{0,j},\tilde{x}_{0,k}), and it vanishes if and only if the clean coefficients are uncorrelated.

Equation (19) is the graph counterpart of blurring diffusion [21], in which the attenuation and the noise variance are a free per-frequency choice with a white terminal law. Here, they follow from the Laplacian-based SDE.

The attenuation and the noise variance (20) state how much of the clean coefficient survives and how much noise replaces it. To compare two graph frequencies, we combine them into the ratio of the retained signal power to the injected noise power, which needs the power at each graph frequency in the clean signal and in the prior. We define the clean power at graph frequency λk\lambda_{k} as the second order moment of the kkth GFT coefficient, pk=𝔼⁡[x~0,k 2]p_{k}=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}_{0,k}^{\,2}], and we call {pk}k=0n−1\{p_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n-1} the power spectrum of the data. Its prior power is the second order moment under the GMRF prior, qk=𝔼⁡[x~∞,k 2]=σ2/λγ,kq_{k}=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}_{\infty,k}^{\,2}]=\sigma^{2}/\lambda_{\gamma,k}, and its power ratio is gk=pk/qk=λγ,k​pk/σ2g_{k}=p_{k}/q_{k}=\lambda_{\gamma,k}p_{k}/\sigma^{2}. The ratio gkg_{k} increases with graph frequency when pkp_{k} decays more slowly than 1/λγ,k1/\lambda_{\gamma,k}.

Definition 2 (Frequency-wise SNR\snr).

For t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T], the frequency-wise SNR at graph frequency λk\lambda_{k} is the power retained from the clean coefficient divided by the variance of the injected noise. Leveraging (20) and gk=λγ,k​pk/σ2g_{k}=\lambda_{\gamma,k}p_{k}/\sigma^{2}, it holds that, under a shared diffusion rate, the SNR is

SNRt,k=at,k2​pkνt,k=gkexp⁡(2​λγ,k​c¯t)−1.\snr_{t,k}=\frac{a_{t,k}^{2}\,p_{k}}{\nu_{t,k}}=\frac{g_{k}}{\exp(2\lambda_{\gamma,k}\bar{c}_{t})-1}. (21)

Definition 2 assigns to each graph frequency the scalar SNR that variational diffusion models attach to a whole noise schedule [28]. The integrated rate is one scalar for all graph frequencies, and SNRt,k\snr_{t,k} depends on it only through the exponent λγ,k​c¯t\lambda_{\gamma,k}\bar{c}_{t}. For two graph frequencies λj\lambda_{j} and λk\lambda_{k} and diffusion time t>0t>0, the ratio of their SNRs factorizes as

SNRt,jSNRt,k=pjpk⏟clean signal⋅λγ,jλγ,k​exp⁡(2​λγ,k​c¯t)−1exp⁡(2​λγ,j​c¯t)−1⏟graph–rate interaction.\frac{\snr_{t,j}}{\snr_{t,k}}=\underbrace{\frac{p_{j}}{p_{k}}}_{\text{clean signal}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,j}}{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}\,\frac{\exp(2\lambda_{\gamma,k}\bar{c}_{t})-1}{\exp(2\lambda_{\gamma,j}\bar{c}_{t})-1}}_{\text{graph--rate interaction}}. (22)

The first factor is the power imbalance present in the clean signal, and no diffusion rate affects it. The second factor tends to one as c¯t→0\bar{c}_{t}\to 0 and, for λγ,j>λγ,k\lambda_{\gamma,j}>\lambda_{\gamma,k}, decays as exp⁡(−2​(λγ,j−λγ,k)​c¯t)\exp(-2(\lambda_{\gamma,j}-\lambda_{\gamma,k})\bar{c}_{t}) once c¯t\bar{c}_{t} is large. A shared diffusion rate therefore separates the SNRs of two graph frequencies exponentially in their gap, and the separation widens for as long as the integrated rate grows. We call this separation the spectral imbalance, and we measure it at diffusion time tt by the spread maxk⁡SNRt,k/mink⁡SNRt,k\max_{k}\snr_{t,k}/\min_{k}\snr_{t,k}. The left panel of Fig. 1 shows the SNRs of different graph frequencies diverging along the horizon.

Reverse. Let the kkth GFT coefficients of the score and of the reverse-time Brownian motion be respectively s~t,k​(𝐱t)=[𝐕𝖳​𝗌t​(𝐱t)]k\tilde{s}_{t,k}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=[\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathsf{s}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})]_{k} and w¯~t,k=[𝐕𝖳​𝐰¯t]k\widetilde{\bar{w}}_{t,k}=[\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{\bar{w}}_{t}]_{k}. Projecting the reverse SDE (15) onto the graph Fourier basis yields

d​x~t,k=[−ct​λγ,k​x~t,k−2​ct​σ2​s~t,k​(𝐱t)]​d​t+2​ct​σ​d​w¯~t,k.d\tilde{x}_{t,k}=\left[-c_{t}\lambda_{\gamma,k}\tilde{x}_{t,k}-2c_{t}\sigma^{2}\,\tilde{s}_{t,k}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right]dt+\sqrt{2c_{t}}\,\sigma\,d\widetilde{\bar{w}}_{t,k}. (23)

Likewise, projecting Tweedie’s formula (16) gives the kkth GFT coefficient of the score,

s~t,k​(𝐱t)=at,k𝔼[x~0,k∣𝐱t,t]−x~t,kνt,k.\tilde{s}_{t,k}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\frac{a_{t,k}\,\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}_{0,k}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t]-\tilde{x}_{t,k}}{\nu_{t,k}}. (24)

The plug-in score s~^t,k\widehat{\tilde{s}}_{t,k} replaces the posterior mean in (24) by the kkth GFT coefficient of the trained denoiser, [𝐕𝖳​fΘ⋆​(𝐱t,𝐋,t)]k[\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}f_{\Theta^{\star}}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{L},t)]_{k}. The attenuation at,ka_{t,k} and the noise variance νt,k\nu_{t,k} therefore appear in two places. First, they fix how much of the clean coefficient is retained in x~t,k\tilde{x}_{t,k}. Second, they convert the denoiser output into the score s~t,k\tilde{s}_{t,k}, which the reverse SDE (23) turns into the drift of that coefficient. The separation of the forward process across graph frequencies does not carry over to the reverse. The posterior mean 𝔼[x~0,k∣𝐱t,t]\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}_{0,k}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t] conditions on the whole vector 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, and it can depend on other GFT coefficients when the clean coefficients are statistically dependent.

IV Spectral Analysis of Denoising Regression

In Section III, we showed that a shared diffusion rate places different graph frequencies at different SNRs at the same diffusion time tt. This matters because GAD learns the score only through the denoiser. By (24), the error of the plug-in score at λk\lambda_{k} is at,k/νt,ka_{t,k}/\nu_{t,k} times the error of the denoiser output with respect to the posterior mean at that frequency, and errors in the score propagate to the reverse drift and from there to the generated samples. The frequency-wise denoising error therefore affects how accurately each graph frequency is generated. In this section, we characterize this error through three quantities: the error attainable at each graph frequency, the time constant at which training reaches that error, and the diffusion times at which the frequency contributes to training. We first consider linear denoisers in Section IV-A. Their minimum error, the linear MMSE, i.e., the MMSE restricted to linear denoisers, is in closed form and coincides with the MMSE for Gaussian data. Section IV-B relates it to the error of a GNN denoiser. Proofs are in Appendix A.

Our analysis relies on the following assumptions.

Assumption 1 (Distinct Laplacian eigenvalues).

The eigenvalues of 𝐋\mathbf{L} are distinct, i.e., 0=λ0<λ1<⋯<λn−10=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}<\cdots<\lambda_{n-1}.

Assumption 2 (Graph wide-sense stationarity [69, 70]).

The covariance of the clean graph signal is diagonal in the graph Fourier basis of (1),

𝐏=Cov⁡(𝐱0)=𝐕​𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀​(p0,…,pn−1)​𝐕𝖳,\mathbf{P}=\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{0})=\mathbf{V}\mathsf{diag}(p_{0},\ldots,p_{n-1})\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}, (25)

with pk=𝔼⁡[x~0,k 2]p_{k}=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}_{0,k}^{\,2}] the clean power at λk\lambda_{k}.

Assumption 1 concerns the graph. We aim to assign an error and a training time constant to each graph frequency, which requires each of them to identify a single eigenvector. When 𝐋\mathbf{L} has repeated eigenvalues, any rotation of the eigenvectors within the eigenspace is also a valid basis and the per-frequency quantities would change with it. Assumption 2 concerns the data. The forward process corrupts each GFT coefficient with noise that is uncorrelated across graph frequencies. For the denoising problem to separate across graph frequencies as well, we need the clean coefficients to be uncorrelated. This implies that the nn powers pkp_{k} fully describe the second-order statistics of 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. Since the error of a linear denoiser depends on (𝐱0,𝐱t)(\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{x}_{t}) only through second moments, Assumption 2 reduces the regression to nn scalar problems, one per GFT coefficient. Without loss of generality, we take 𝔼⁡[𝐱0]=𝟎\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}]=\mathbf{0}, as the training data are centered. Throughout, we fix t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T] and consider the fixed-time denoising error

ℒt​(f)=𝔼⁡[‖𝐱0−f⁡(𝐱t)‖22|t],\mathcal{L}_{t}(f)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\mathbf{x}_{0}-f(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\,\middle|\,t\right], (26)

which (17) averages over the diffusion time.

IV-A Linear Denoisers

Consider the linear denoiser f𝐖​(𝐱t)=𝐖𝐱tf_{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_{t} with 𝐖∈ℝn×n\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. This class contains the graph convolutional filter (2), the spectral graph filter (4), and the GNN (5) with identity nonlinearity. We characterize three quantities per graph frequency: (i) the error of the optimal linear denoiser, (ii) the rate at which gradient descent converges to it, and (iii) the diffusion times at which it contributes to the fixed-time error ℒt\mathcal{L}_{t}. All three depend on the second moment of the kkth corrupted GFT coefficient,

ρt,k=𝔼⁡[x~t,k 2]=at,k2​pk+νt,k=at,k2​pk+(1−at,k2)​qk>0,\rho_{t,k}=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}_{t,k}^{\,2}]=a_{t,k}^{2}p_{k}+\nu_{t,k}=a_{t,k}^{2}p_{k}+\bigl(1-a_{t,k}^{2}\bigr)q_{k}>0, (27)

which we call the corrupted power. It is a convex combination of the clean power pkp_{k} and the prior power qkq_{k}.

Optimal linear denoiser. Under Assumption 2, the corrupted GFT coefficients are uncorrelated across graph frequencies, and the minimizer of ℒt​(f𝐖)\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{\mathbf{W}}) is the spectral graph filter

f𝐡t​(𝐱t)=𝐕​𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀​(𝐡t)​𝐕𝖳​𝐱tf_{\mathbf{h}_{t}}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\mathbf{V}\mathsf{diag}(\mathbf{h}_{t})\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x}_{t} (28)

with frequency response

ht,k⋆=at,k​pkρt,k=1at,kSNRt,k1+SNRt,k,k=0,…,n−1h_{t,k}^{\star}=\frac{a_{t,k}p_{k}}{\rho_{t,k}}=\frac{1}{a_{t,k}}\frac{\snr_{t,k}}{1+\snr_{t,k}},\quad k=0,\ldots,n-1 (29)

(Lemma 1). This is the Wiener filter of the scalar Gaussian model for x~t,k\tilde{x}_{t,k}, which inverts the attenuation at,ka_{t,k} and scales the result by a factor that decreases with the SNR. Each clean coefficient x~0,k\tilde{x}_{0,k} is estimated from its own corrupted coefficient x~t,k\tilde{x}_{t,k}, and the error of this denoiser is formalized next.

Proposition 1 (Frequency-wise normalized error).

Let Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, let t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T], and pk>0p_{k}>0. Then, at λk\lambda_{k} the optimal linear denoiser (28)–(29) yields the normalized error

dt,k=𝔼⁡[(x~0,k−ht,k⋆​x~t,k)2|t]pk=11+SNRt,k.d_{t,k}=\frac{\mathbb{E}\!\left[(\tilde{x}_{0,k}-h_{t,k}^{\star}\tilde{x}_{t,k})^{2}\,\middle|\,t\right]}{p_{k}}=\frac{1}{1+\snr_{t,k}}. (30)

Summing over graph frequencies gives the linear MMSE, i.e., the minimum fixed-time error over linear denoisers,

ℬt=min𝐖⁡ℒt​(f𝐖)=∑k=0n−1pk​dt,k.\mathcal{B}_{t}=\min_{\mathbf{W}}\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{\mathbf{W}})=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}p_{k}\,d_{t,k}. (31)

Both the normalized error dt,kd_{t,k} and the linear MMSE ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} depend on at,ka_{t,k} and νt,k\nu_{t,k} only through SNRt,k\snr_{t,k}. The normalized error dt,kd_{t,k} goes from zero for SNRt,k≫1\snr_{t,k}\gg 1 to one for SNRt,k≪1\snr_{t,k}\ll 1. Because of the spectral imbalance (22), once c¯t\bar{c}_{t} is large enough for the exponential factor to dominate the power ratio pj/pkp_{j}/p_{k}, a shared diffusion rate keeps the highest graph frequencies at the lowest SNR, so they contribute pk​dt,k≈pkp_{k}d_{t,k}\approx p_{k} to ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t}. Reducing ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} requires a higher SNR at these graph frequencies, which a shared diffusion rate can achieve only by reducing c¯t\bar{c}_{t}. This raises the SNR at all graph frequencies at that time. Keeping c¯T\bar{c}_{T} fixed then shifts part of the corruption to later times.

Training time constant. Under a finite number of training iterations, a graph frequency whose frequency response is still far from ht,k⋆h_{t,k}^{\star} still has a larger error, so we want to characterize how fast it converges. Since the minimizer is a spectral graph filter, we train the n×1n\times 1 frequency response 𝐡t\mathbf{h}_{t} within this class using gradient descent with learning rate η>0\eta>0. At fixed diffusion time tt, we study the gradient flow d​𝐡t/d​τ=−η​∇𝐡tℒt​(f𝐡t)d\mathbf{h}_{t}/d\tau=-\eta\nabla_{\mathbf{h}_{t}}\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{\mathbf{h}_{t}}), where τ\tau is optimization time and η>0\eta>0.

Proposition 2 (Frequency-wise training time constant).

Let Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, let t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T], and let the frequency response 𝐡t​(τ)\mathbf{h}_{t}(\tau) follow the gradient flow introduced above from any initialization 𝐡t​(0)\mathbf{h}_{t}(0). Then, the frequency response at each graph frequency converges to ht,k⋆h_{t,k}^{\star} in (29) independently of the others,

ht,k(τ)−ht,k⋆=e−τ/τt,k(ht,k(0)−ht,k⋆),τt,k=(2ηρt,k)−1,h_{t,k}(\tau)-h_{t,k}^{\star}=e^{-\tau/\tau_{t,k}}\bigl(h_{t,k}(0)-h_{t,k}^{\star}\bigr),\quad\tau_{t,k}=\bigl(2\eta\,\rho_{t,k}\bigr)^{-1}, (32)

where τt,k\tau_{t,k} is the training time constant at λk\lambda_{k}.

The training time constant at λk\lambda_{k} depends only on the corrupted power ρt,k\rho_{t,k}, hence the graph frequencies are learned in decreasing order of that power. This is the spectral bias of diffusion training [49], and under GAD the diffusion rate sets it through the attenuation at,ka_{t,k} in ρt,k\rho_{t,k}. Training all graph frequencies to the same accuracy requires waiting for the slowest one, which takes maxk⁡ρt,k/mink⁡ρt,k\max_{k}\rho_{t,k}/\min_{k}\rho_{t,k} times longer than the fastest. We call this ratio the spread of the training time constants. As at,k→0a_{t,k}\to 0 for all kk, the corrupted powers approach the prior powers qkq_{k}, and the spread tends to the condition number of the shifted Laplacian, cond⁡(𝐋γ)=(λn−1+γ)/γ\cond(\mathbf{L}_{\gamma})=(\lambda_{n-1}+\gamma)/\gamma. We call this limit the terminal spread, with the highest graph frequency being the slowest. This limit depends only on 𝐋γ\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}.

Informative graph frequencies. Propositions 1 and 2 hold at a fixed diffusion time, whereas training samples tt over the whole horizon. By Proposition 1, a graph frequency with SNRt,k≫1\snr_{t,k}\gg 1 has dt,k≈0d_{t,k}\approx 0 and one with SNRt,k≪1\snr_{t,k}\ll 1 has dt,k≈1d_{t,k}\approx 1. The optimal linear response approximately inverts the attenuation at high SNR and approaches the prior-mean estimate at low SNR [46, 47]. We therefore investigate which graph frequencies a shared diffusion rate keeps at a moderate SNR, and when.

Definition 3 (ε\varepsilon-informative graph frequency).

Let ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) be a tolerance. Graph frequency λk\lambda_{k} is ε\varepsilon-informative at diffusion time tt if SNRt,k∈[ε,ε−1]\snr_{t,k}\in[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}].

We call the set of ε\varepsilon-informative graph frequencies at time tt, {λk:SNRt,k∈[ε,ε−1]}\{\lambda_{k}:\snr_{t,k}\in[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]\}, the informative band. Graph frequencies with SNRt,k>ε−1\snr_{t,k}>\varepsilon^{-1} are preserved at time tt, and those with SNRt,k<ε\snr_{t,k}<\varepsilon are lost. The value of SNRt,k\snr_{t,k} decreases strictly in c¯t\bar{c}_{t}, so graph frequency λk\lambda_{k} is informative on a single interval of integrated-rate values, of length at most log⁡(1/ε)/λγ,k\log(1/\varepsilon)/\lambda_{\gamma,k} (Lemma 2). If pkp_{k} is nonincreasing with graph frequency, these intervals start earlier and are shorter at higher frequencies. Their probability under the training law depends on both c¯t\bar{c}_{t} and πtr\pi_{\mathrm{tr}}. The next proposition bounds the width of this band.

Proposition 3 (Informative band).

Let the diffusion rate be shared, let pk>0p_{k}>0 for all kk, and let gmin=mink⁡gkg_{\min}=\min_{k}g_{k} and gmax=maxk⁡gkg_{\max}=\max_{k}g_{k}. Then, any two graph frequencies λj\lambda_{j} and λk\lambda_{k} that are ε\varepsilon-informative at the same diffusion time satisfy

λγ,jλγ,k≤log⁡(1+gmax​ε−1)log⁡(1+gmin​ε).\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,j}}{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}\;\leq\;\frac{\log\bigl(1+g_{\max}\varepsilon^{-1}\bigr)}{\log\bigl(1+g_{\min}\varepsilon\bigr)}. (33)

The bound constrains the band when it is smaller than cond⁡(𝐋γ)\cond(\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}). With a shared diffusion rate, all graph frequencies can be informative at the same time, but distinct frequencies cannot maintain equal SNRs over a time interval. This motivates our design in Section V.

IV-B GNN Denoiser

In practice, GAD trains the time-conditioned GNN fΘ​(𝐱t,𝐋,t)f_{\Theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{L},t) of (5), whose output at each graph frequency can depend on the whole vector 𝐱~t\mathbf{\tilde{x}}_{t}. We analyze its fixed-time error ℒt​(fΘ)\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{\Theta}) by comparing the GNN with two estimators: the posterior mean 𝗆t(𝐱)=𝔼[𝐱0∣𝐱t=𝐱,t]\mathsf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{x},t], whose error is the MMSE, and the optimal linear denoiser ht,k⋆h_{t,k}^{\star}, whose error is the linear MMSE ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t}.

Proposition 4 (GNN error decomposition).

Let Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, let t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T], and let mt,k=[𝐕𝖳​𝗆t​(𝐱t)]km_{t,k}=[\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathsf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})]_{k} and x~^0,k=[𝐕𝖳​fΘ​(𝐱t,𝐋,t)]k\widehat{\tilde{x}}_{0,k}=[\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}f_{\Theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{L},t)]_{k} be the kkth GFT coefficients of the posterior mean and of the GNN output. Then, the fixed-time error ℒt​(fΘ)\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{\Theta}) of the GNN decomposes as

ℒt​(fΘ)=ℬt−ΔPM,t+ΩΘ,t,\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{\Theta})=\mathcal{B}_{t}-\Delta_{\mathrm{PM},t}+\Omega_{\Theta,t}, (34)

where ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} is the linear MMSE,

ΔPM,t=∑k=0n−1Δt,k,Δt,k=𝔼⁡[(mt,k−ht,k⋆​x~t,k)2|t]≥0\Delta_{\mathrm{PM},t}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\Delta_{t,k},\qquad\Delta_{t,k}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(m_{t,k}-h_{t,k}^{\star}\tilde{x}_{t,k})^{2}\,\middle|\,t\right]\geq 0

is the gain of the posterior mean over the optimal linear denoiser ht,k⋆h_{t,k}^{\star}, with Δt,k\Delta_{t,k} its frequency-wise term, and

ΩΘ,t=∑k=0n−1𝔼⁡[(mt,k−x~^0,k)2|t]≥0\Omega_{\Theta,t}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(m_{t,k}-\widehat{\tilde{x}}_{0,k})^{2}\,\middle|\,t\right]\geq 0

is the error of the GNN with respect to the posterior mean.

The posterior-mean gain ΔPM,t\Delta_{\mathrm{PM},t} measures the improvement over the optimal linear denoiser. It depends on the data law and the corruption, vanishing for Gaussian data under graph stationarity. Let mt,ksc=𝔼[x~0,k∣x~t,k,t]m^{\mathrm{sc}}_{t,k}=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}_{0,k}\mid\tilde{x}_{t,k},t] be the posterior mean given only the kkth corrupted coefficient. Then

Δt,k=𝔼⁡[(mt,k−mt,ksc)2∣t]+𝔼⁡[(mt,ksc−ht,k⋆​x~t,k)2∣t].\displaystyle\Delta_{t,k}=\,\mathbb{E}[(m_{t,k}-m^{\mathrm{sc}}_{t,k})^{2}\mid t]\,+\,\mathbb{E}[(m^{\mathrm{sc}}_{t,k}-h^{\star}_{t,k}\tilde{x}_{t,k})^{2}\mid t].

The first term is the gain from observing the other corrupted GFT coefficients, and the second is the nonlinear gain from the kkth coefficient alone. The excess error ΩΘ,t\Omega_{\Theta,t} includes approximation and optimization error and is the only term that depends on the GNN parameters. This decomposition follows from orthogonality (Lemma 3), which also gives the second moment of the posterior mean at each graph frequency.

Corollary 1 (Second moment of the posterior mean).

Let Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, let t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T], and let pk>0p_{k}>0. Then, the second moment of the posterior mean mt,km_{t,k} at λk\lambda_{k} is

𝔼⁡[mt,k2|t]=pk​SNRt,k1+SNRt,k+Δt,k,\mathbb{E}\!\left[m_{t,k}^{2}\,\middle|\,t\right]=p_{k}\frac{\snr_{t,k}}{1+\snr_{t,k}}+\Delta_{t,k}, (35)

where Δt,k\Delta_{t,k} is the frequency-wise gain of Proposition 4.

The first term in (35) is the energy of the optimal linear estimate from x~t,k\tilde{x}_{t,k}. The second, Δt,k\Delta_{t,k}, combines the gain from observing the corrupted coefficients x~t,j\tilde{x}_{t,j} with j≠kj\neq k and the gain from estimating x~0,k\tilde{x}_{0,k} nonlinearly from x~t,k\tilde{x}_{t,k} alone.

Proposition 2 does not carry over directly to the GNN. At a fixed diffusion time, off-diagonal entries of its tangent kernel can arise from the nonlinearity ϕ\mathsf{\phi} and from parameters shared across graph frequencies (Appendix B). The shared parameters also couple different diffusion times during training.

For low-pass data under a shared diffusion rate, the high graph frequencies are informative over shorter ranges of integrated rates. Near the prior, their fixed-time linear training constants are the largest.

V Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling

In this section, we design diffusion rates that remove the spectral imbalance identified in Section IV. Three quantities from that section depend on the diffusion rate only through the frequency-wise SNR: the normalized linear error dt,kd_{t,k}, whether a frequency is informative, and the energy of its optimal linear estimate as a fraction of clean power. Equalizing the SNR equalizes all three. A shared diffusion rate cannot maintain this equality over a time interval for distinct eigenvalues. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and imposes a common target SNR on all of them. A frequency-dependent diffusion rate does not change the process that each GFT coefficient follows. It only reparametrizes the diffusion time of that coefficient through its integrated rate c¯t,k\bar{c}_{t,k}. As a result, the GMRF prior is preserved, and MASS synchronizes the graph frequencies along the forward process rather than replacing it. Section V-A derives the diffusion rates, Section V-B analyzes their effect on training and sampling, and Section V-C gives the resulting algorithms and their cost. Proofs are in Appendix C.

V-A MASS Diffusion Rates

A diffusion rate per graph frequency requires a single eigenvector for each of them, which Assumption 1 provides. Let ct,k≥0c_{t,k}\geq 0 be the diffusion rate at λk\lambda_{k} and c¯t,k=∫0tcs,k​𝑑s\bar{c}_{t,k}=\int_{0}^{t}c_{s,k}\,ds its integrated rate. We collect them in the graph operator 𝐂t=𝐕​𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀​(ct,0,…,ct,n−1)​𝐕𝖳\mathbf{C}_{t}=\mathbf{V}\mathsf{diag}(c_{t,0},\ldots,c_{t,n-1})\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}} and replace the scalar ctc_{t} of the forward SDE (10) by this operator,

d​𝐱t=−𝐂t​𝐋γ​𝐱t​d​t+2​σ​𝐂t1/2​d​𝐰t.d\mathbf{x}_{t}=-\mathbf{C}_{t}\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}\mathbf{x}_{t}\,dt+\sqrt{2}\,\sigma\,\mathbf{C}_{t}^{1/2}d\mathbf{w}_{t}. (36)

Since 𝐂t\mathbf{C}_{t} and 𝐋γ\mathbf{L}_{\gamma} are diagonal in the same basis, each GFT coefficient still follows (19), with c¯t\bar{c}_{t} replaced by c¯t,k\bar{c}_{t,k} in at,ka_{t,k} and νt,k\nu_{t,k}. A frequency-dependent diffusion rate changes how quickly each GFT coefficient evolves, but not its stationary distribution. The GMRF prior therefore remains (13). Let rt>0r_{t}>0 be a continuously differentiable, decreasing target SNR on (0,T](0,T], satisfying limt→0+rt=+∞\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}r_{t}=+\infty and rT=rmin>0r_{T}=r_{\min}>0. We exclude t=0t=0, where no noise has been injected and the SNR is undefined. We require the SNR at every graph frequency to follow this target,

SNRt,k=rt,k=0,…,n−1.\snr_{t,k}=r_{t},\qquad k=0,\ldots,n-1. (37)
Theorem 1 (MASS diffusion rates).

Let Assumption 1 hold, let pk>0p_{k}>0 for all kk, and let the target SNR rt>0r_{t}>0 be continuously differentiable and decreasing on (0,T](0,T], with limt→0+rt=+∞\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}r_{t}=+\infty. Then, the constraint (37) uniquely determines the frequency-wise integrated rates

c¯t,k=12​λγ,k​log⁡(1+gkrt).\bar{c}_{t,k}=\frac{1}{2\lambda_{\gamma,k}}\log\!\left(1+\frac{g_{k}}{r_{t}}\right). (38)

Each integrated rate is nonnegative and nondecreasing in tt, and c¯t,k→0\bar{c}_{t,k}\to 0 as t→0+t\to 0^{+} (equivalently, as rt→∞r_{t}\to\infty). The corresponding diffusion rate is

ct,k=−12​λγ,k​gkrt+gk​dd​t​log⁡rt≥ 0.c_{t,k}=-\frac{1}{2\lambda_{\gamma,k}}\frac{g_{k}}{r_{t}+g_{k}}\frac{d}{dt}\log r_{t}\;\geq\;0. (39)

The rate in (39) is approximately proportional to pkp_{k} when rt≫gkr_{t}\gg g_{k} and approximately inversely proportional to λγ,k\lambda_{\gamma,k} when rt≪gkr_{t}\ll g_{k}. Substituting (38) into (20) and using qk​gk=pkq_{k}g_{k}=p_{k} gives, under MASS,

at,k2=rtrt+gk,νt,k\displaystyle a_{t,k}^{2}=\frac{r_{t}}{r_{t}+g_{k}},~~\nu_{t,k} =pkrt+gk,ρt,k=(1+rt)​νt,k.\displaystyle=\frac{p_{k}}{r_{t}+g_{k}},~\rho_{t,k}=(1+r_{t})\,\nu_{t,k}. (40)

The attenuation at,ka_{t,k} and the normalized noise variance νt,k/pk\nu_{t,k}/p_{k} depend on the graph frequency only through the power ratio gk=pk/qkg_{k}=p_{k}/q_{k}, which compares the power of the data at λk\lambda_{k} with the power that the GMRF prior already assigns to it. Graph frequencies at which the data carry more power than the prior require more attenuation to reach the common SNR rtr_{t}, and those well explained by the prior require less. MASS thus sets the corruption of each graph frequency from the interplay between the graph and the data.

Target SNR. Since rtr_{t} diverges at t=0t=0, we run the process on [t0,T][t_{0},T] with finite endpoints rt0=rmaxr_{t_{0}}=r_{\max} and rT=rminr_{T}=r_{\min}. From here on, the horizon is [t0,T][t_{0},T], and the training law πtr\pi_{\mathrm{tr}} is supported on it. We set tolerances on the fraction of clean power retained by each GFT coefficient, requiring at0,k2≥1−δ0a_{t_{0},k}^{2}\geq 1-\delta_{0} and aT,k2≤δa_{T,k}^{2}\leq\delta for every kk, with a start tolerance δ0∈(0,1)\delta_{0}\in(0,1) and a tolerance δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). The latter is the δ\delta-completeness of Definition 1 applied at each graph frequency. By (40), these conditions hold if and only if rmax≥gmax​(1−δ0)/δ0r_{\max}\geq g_{\max}(1-\delta_{0})/\delta_{0} and rmin≤gmin​δ/(1−δ)r_{\min}\leq g_{\min}\delta/(1-\delta), with gmax=maxk⁡gkg_{\max}=\max_{k}g_{k} and gmin=mink⁡gkg_{\min}=\min_{k}g_{k}, hence the target SNR must span

rmaxrmin≥1−δ0δ0​1−δδ​gmaxgmin.\frac{r_{\max}}{r_{\min}}\;\geq\;\frac{1-\delta_{0}}{\delta_{0}}\,\frac{1-\delta}{\delta}\,\frac{g_{\max}}{g_{\min}}. (41)

The target SNR depends on the graph only through this span. Between the endpoints, rtr_{t} can be chosen freely, and we let the log-SNR decrease linearly in time,

log⁡rt=(1−ut)​log⁡rmax+ut​log⁡rmin,\log r_{t}=(1-u_{t})\log r_{\max}+u_{t}\log r_{\min}, (42)

where utu_{t} increases from ut0=0u_{t_{0}}=0 to uT=1u_{T}=1. Finally, MASS needs the clean powers pkp_{k}. We center the NN training signals, estimate

p^k=1N​∑i=1N(𝐯k𝖳​𝐱0(i))2,p^k←max⁡(p^k,pmin),\widehat{p}_{k}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x}_{0}^{(i)}\right)^{2},\qquad\widehat{p}_{k}\leftarrow\max(\widehat{p}_{k},p_{\min}), (43)

with pmin>0p_{\min}>0, and add the mean back after sampling. The floor keeps the estimated power ratios positive. Using the floored powers p^k\widehat{p}_{k}, the SNR attained is SNRt,k=rt​pk/p^k\snr_{t,k}=r_{t}\,p_{k}/\widehat{p}_{k}.

V-B Effect on Training and Sampling

Training. With SNRt,k=rt\snr_{t,k}=r_{t} for all kk, Proposition 1 gives the same normalized error dt,k=1/(1+rt)d_{t,k}=1/(1+r_{t}) at every graph frequency, and the linear MMSE ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} becomes 𝔼​‖𝐱0‖22/(1+rt)\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{x}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}/(1+r_{t}), which depends on the data only through the total power ∑kpk\sum_{k}p_{k} and does not depend on the Laplacian. Every graph frequency is ε\varepsilon-informative on the same set of diffusion times {t:ε≤rt≤ε−1}\{t:\varepsilon\leq r_{t}\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\}, so the informative band then covers all of them. The energy of the optimal linear estimate is the same fraction rt/(1+rt)r_{t}/(1+r_{t}) of the clean power at every graph frequency. Under MASS, the posterior-mean gain depends on diffusion time only through rtr_{t}.

Sampling. The spectral imbalance can also affect the stiffness of the reverse SDE. To study step-size restrictions for explicit solvers [71, 72], we write the reverse drift in the GFT basis. Let f~Θ​(𝐱~,t)=𝐕𝖳​fΘ​(𝐕​𝐱~,𝐋,t)\tilde{f}_{\Theta}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}},t)=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}f_{\Theta}(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{\tilde{x}},\mathbf{L},t) be the denoiser in this basis, with kkth coefficient f~Θ,k​(𝐱~,t)\tilde{f}_{\Theta,k}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}},t), and let s~^t,k​(𝐱~)=(at,k​f~Θ,k​(𝐱~,t)−x~k)/νt,k\widehat{\tilde{s}}_{t,k}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}})=(a_{t,k}\tilde{f}_{\Theta,k}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}},t)-\tilde{x}_{k})/\nu_{t,k} be the plug-in score obtained by replacing the posterior mean in s~t,k\tilde{s}_{t,k} with f~Θ,k​(𝐱~,t)\tilde{f}_{\Theta,k}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}},t). Substituting the latter into the reverse SDE (23) with diffusion rate ct,kc_{t,k}, and using σ2/νt,k=λγ,k/(1−at,k2)\sigma^{2}/\nu_{t,k}=\lambda_{\gamma,k}/(1-a_{t,k}^{2}) from (20), gives the reverse drift of the kkth GFT coefficient,

b~t,k​(𝐱~)=ct,k​λγ,k1−at,k2⏟reverse-time gain​[(1+at,k2)​x~k−2​at,k​f~Θ,k​(𝐱~,t)]⏟denoising direction.\tilde{b}_{t,k}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}})=\underbrace{c_{t,k}\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}{1-a_{t,k}^{2}}}_{\text{reverse-time gain}}\underbrace{\Bigl[(1+a_{t,k}^{2})\tilde{x}_{k}-2a_{t,k}\tilde{f}_{\Theta,k}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}},t)\Bigr]}_{\text{denoising direction}}. (44)

The reverse-time gain scales the magnitude of the drift of the kkth GFT coefficient, and the denoising direction determines its sign and its dependence on the denoiser output. For a spectral graph filter with frequency response ht,kh_{t,k}, we have f~Θ,k​(𝐱~,t)=ht,k​x~k\tilde{f}_{\Theta,k}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}},t)=h_{t,k}\tilde{x}_{k}, and the drift reduces to

b~t,k​(𝐱~)=ζt,k​x~k,ζt,k=ct,k​λγ,k​1+at,k2−2​at,k​ht,k1−at,k2.\tilde{b}_{t,k}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}})=\zeta_{t,k}\tilde{x}_{k},\qquad\zeta_{t,k}=c_{t,k}\lambda_{\gamma,k}\frac{1+a_{t,k}^{2}-2a_{t,k}h_{t,k}}{1-a_{t,k}^{2}}. (45)

We call ζt,k\zeta_{t,k} the local stiffness at λk\lambda_{k}. For a nonlinear denoiser, the GFT coefficients are coupled. The drift 𝐛~t\mathbf{\tilde{b}}_{t}, which collects (44) over kk, depends on the whole vector 𝐱~\mathbf{\tilde{x}}, and the eigenvalues of its Jacobian ∇𝐱~𝐛~t\nabla_{\mathbf{\tilde{x}}}\mathbf{\tilde{b}}_{t} govern local linear stability. We summarize the scale of this Jacobian by

LS=supt∈[t0,T]sup𝐱~∈ℛt‖∇𝐱~𝐛~t​(𝐱~)‖2,L_{S}=\sup_{t\in[t_{0},T]}\sup_{\mathbf{\tilde{x}}\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}\left\|\nabla_{\mathbf{\tilde{x}}}\mathbf{\tilde{b}}_{t}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}})\right\|_{2}, (46)

where ℛt⊂ℝn\mathcal{R}_{t}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is any set containing the vectors the sampler can reach at time tt, and we call LSL_{S} the reverse-time stiffness. For the spectral graph filter, the Jacobian is 𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀⁡(ζt,0,…,ζt,n−1)\mathsf{diag}(\zeta_{t,0},\ldots,\zeta_{t,n-1}) and LS=supt∈[t0,T]maxk⁡|ζt,k|L_{S}=\sup_{t\in[t_{0},T]}\max_{k}|\zeta_{t,k}|. For an explicit reverse-SDE solver, the local linear stability test uses the eigenvalues of the drift Jacobian scaled by −Δ​t-\Delta t. For a given time parametrization, we use LSL_{S} as a proxy for the step-size restriction.

MASS makes the reverse-time gain identical at every graph frequency. Substituting (39) and (40) gives ct,kλγ,k/(1−at,k2)=−12dlogrt/dtc_{t,k}\lambda_{\gamma,k}/(1-a_{t,k}^{2})=-\tfrac{1}{2}\,d\log r_{t}/dt, and the supremum of the common gain is M/2M/2, where M=supt∈[t0,T]|d​log⁡rt/d​t|M=\sup_{t\in[t_{0},T]}|d\log r_{t}/dt|. Among the target SNRs (42) that join rmaxr_{\max} to rminr_{\min}, a linear utu_{t} has the smallest log-SNR slope, M=log⁡(rmax/rmin)/(T−t0)M=\log(r_{\max}/r_{\min})/(T-t_{0}), since a supremum is at least an average. The Jacobian also depends on the sensitivity of the denoiser to 𝐱~\mathbf{\tilde{x}}, which can grow with the spectral radius through the powers of 𝐋\mathbf{L} used by the GNN. We isolate this sensitivity.

Assumption 3 (Bounded attenuated Jacobian).

There exists a constant B<∞B<\infty, independent of the eigenvalues of 𝐋γ\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}, such that ‖𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀⁡(𝐚t)​∇𝐱~f~Θ​(𝐱~,t)‖2≤B\bigl\|\mathsf{diag}(\mathbf{a}_{t})\nabla_{\mathbf{\tilde{x}}}\tilde{f}_{\Theta}(\mathbf{\tilde{x}},t)\bigr\|_{2}\leq B for all 𝐱~∈ℛt\mathbf{\tilde{x}}\in\mathcal{R}_{t} and t∈[t0,T]t\in[t_{0},T].

For the spectral filter ht,k⋆h_{t,k}^{\star}, which is the optimal linear denoiser under Assumption 2, the matrix in Assumption 3 is diagonal with entries at,k​ht,k⋆=SNRt,k/(1+SNRt,k)<1a_{t,k}h_{t,k}^{\star}=\snr_{t,k}/(1+\snr_{t,k})<1, hence one can take B=1B=1 for this filter. For a trained GNN, BB depends on the trained weights, the attenuations and the set ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}.

Theorem 2 (MASS stiffness bound).

Let Assumptions 1 and 3 hold, and let LSMASSL_{S}^{\mathrm{MASS}} be the reverse-time stiffness (46) under the MASS diffusion rates (38). Then,

LSMASS≤M⁡(1+B),M=supt∈[t0,T]|dd​t​log⁡rt|,L_{S}^{\mathrm{MASS}}\leq M(1+B),\qquad M=\sup_{t\in[t_{0},T]}\left|\frac{d}{dt}\log r_{t}\right|, (47)

where MM is the log-SNR slope and BB is the constant in Assumption 3.

If, in addition, the endpoints rmaxr_{\max} and rminr_{\min} satisfy (41) with equality for δ0=δ∈(0,1/2)\delta_{0}=\delta\in(0,1/2), the target SNR follows (42) with the linear ramp ut=(t−t0)/(T−t0)u_{t}=(t-t_{0})/(T-t_{0}), and maxk⁡pk≤κ​mink​pk\max_{k}p_{k}\leq\kappa\min_{k}p_{k} for some κ≥1\kappa\geq 1, then

LSMASS≤1+BT−t0​[2​log⁡−δδ+log⁡κ+log⁡cond⁡(𝐋γ)].\!L_{S}^{\mathrm{MASS}}\leq\frac{1+B}{T-t_{0}}\!\Big[2\log\frac{1\!-\!\delta}{\delta}+\log\kappa+\log\cond(\mathbf{L}_{\gamma})\!\Big]\!. (48)

For fixed BB, the bound depends on the graph through the log-SNR slope MM. For comparison, under a shared, nondecreasing diffusion rate, a δ\delta-complete horizon with SNRT,n−1≤1/3\snr_{T,n-1}\leq 1/3, and the optimal linear denoiser ht,k⋆h_{t,k}^{\star}, the reverse-time stiffness satisfies LSshared≥log⁡(1/δ)​cond⁡(𝐋γ)/(4​T)L_{S}^{\mathrm{shared}}\geq\log(1/\delta)\cond(\mathbf{L}_{\gamma})/(4T) (Proposition 5 in Appendix C). For fixed δ\delta, horizon, BB and κ\kappa, the two bounds scale as

LSMASS=𝖮⁡(log⁡cond⁡(𝐋γ)),LSshared=Ω⁡(cond⁡(𝐋γ)).L_{S}^{\mathrm{MASS}}=\mathsf{O}\!\left(\log\cond(\mathbf{L}_{\gamma})\right),~L_{S}^{\mathrm{shared}}=\Omega\!\left(\cond(\mathbf{L}_{\gamma})\right). (49)

Under a shared diffusion rate, δ\delta-completeness imposes an integrated rate at the lowest graph frequency, which contributes to the stiffness at the highest frequency. Under MASS, the attenuation tolerances instead determine the required span rmax/rminr_{\max}/r_{\min}.

V-C Algorithms and Complexity

Algorithm 1 trains through the closed-form MASS attenuation at,ka_{t,k} and noise variance νt,k\nu_{t,k} (40), and Algorithm 2 integrates the reverse SDE in the graph Fourier domain by Euler–Maruyama with exactly integrated noise variance at each step. Both use the floored estimate p^k\widehat{p}_{k} and g^k=λγ,k​p^k/σ2\widehat{g}_{k}=\lambda_{\gamma,k}\widehat{p}_{k}/\sigma^{2}. The sampler uses a diagonal Gaussian approximation to the terminal marginal and returns 𝐱t0\mathbf{x}_{t_{0}}.

Table II reports the computational cost of GAD-MASS, where 𝒞Θtrain\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{train}}_{\Theta} and 𝒞Θeval\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{eval}}_{\Theta} denote the cost of one training pass and of one denoiser evaluation, respectively. Two operations are performed only once. The first is the eigendecomposition of 𝐋γ\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}, which GAD requires anyway. The second is the estimation of the power spectrum p^k\widehat{p}_{k}, which costs 𝖮⁡(N​n2)\mathsf{O}(Nn^{2}) and is dominated by the eigendecomposition whenever N≲nN\lesssim n. After this, MASS only adds the frequency-wise attenuation at,ka_{t,k} and noise variance νt,k\nu_{t,k} at each diffusion time. This is an elementwise operation of cost 𝖮⁡(n)\mathsf{O}(n), which is negligible compared with the 𝖮⁡(n2)\mathsf{O}(n^{2}) GFT and inverse GFT that the algorithms perform at every step. We finally note that MASS adds no trainable parameters.

VI Numerical Analysis

In this section, we test our theoretical results on synthetic data in Section VI-A and evaluate GAD with MASS on three real-data case studies, namely collaborative recommendation, traffic imputation and probabilistic spatio-temporal forecasting, in Section VI-B. Overall, GAD with MASS matches or improves the state of the art in all three tasks with a fraction of the reverse steps.

VI-A Synthetic Experiments

We test Theorem 1, Proposition 5 and Theorem 2 on a synthetic graph and synthetic data.

Setup. We use a random geometric 88-nearest-neighbor graph with n=128n=128 nodes and Gaussian edge weights. The Gaussian weights make the eigenvalues distinct, as Assumption 1 requires. We draw two Gaussian datasets of 10,00010{,}000 training, 2,0002{,}000 validation and 2,0002{,}000 test signals.

  • •

    The stationary signal satisfies Assumption 2 and tests MASS where the theory is exact. Its GFT coefficients are independent, x~0,k∼𝒩⁡(0,pk)\tilde{x}_{0,k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,p_{k}), with pk∝(0.05+λk/λn−1)−3/2+24.8p_{k}\propto(0.05+\lambda_{k}/\lambda_{n-1})^{-3/2}+24.8 scaled to unit mean power. The power-law term concentrates the power at the low graph frequencies, and the offset 24.824.8 raises the share of the highest quarter of the graph frequencies to 20%20\%, so that the metrics are sensitive to the graph frequencies that a shared diffusion rate loses first (22). The power spectrum uses the eigenvalues of 𝐋\mathbf{L}, not of 𝐋γ\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}, so that a change of the shift does not change the data. It is much flatter than the prior power σ2/λγ,k\sigma^{2}/\lambda_{\gamma,k}, hence gkg_{k} varies across graph frequencies and MASS does not reduce to an equal attenuation (40).

  • •

    The block-covariance signal has four groups of 3232 nodes with unit variance and a correlation of 0.80.8 within a group. Its covariance is specified in the vertex domain, hence it does not commute with 𝐋γ\mathbf{L}_{\gamma} and violates Assumption 2.

Forward processes. We compare MASS (38) with three baselines. FCPS, the floor-constrained polynomial schedule of our preliminary work [25], is the shared GAD diffusion rate that MASS replaces, c¯t=cmin​t+(c¯T−cmin​T)​(t/T)α+1\bar{c}_{t}=c_{\min}t+(\bar{c}_{T}-c_{\min}T)(t/T)^{\alpha+1}. Cosine is the shared GAD diffusion rate whose integrated rate follows the logarithm of the signal fraction of the cosine schedule [43], with offset scs_{\mathrm{c}} and endpoint truncation tct_{\mathrm{c}}. Both have a nondecreasing diffusion rate ctc_{t}, as Proposition 5 assumes. The isotropic variance-preserving (VP) baseline [3], the forward process of the downstream pipelines, has the cosine signal fraction in every direction and no Laplacian in its forward process, and keeps the graph-aware denoiser. Every forward process retains at most a fraction δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3} of the clean power at TT (Definition 1), and the shared diffusion rates use c¯T=log⁡(1/δ)/(2​γ)\bar{c}_{T}=\log(1/\delta)/(2\gamma). MASS sets rmax=gmax​(1−δ0)/δ0r_{\max}=g_{\max}(1-\delta_{0})/\delta_{0} and rmin=gmin​δ/(1−δ)r_{\min}=g_{\min}\delta/(1-\delta), the endpoint conditions of Section V-A at equality, and uses the cosine ramp ut=12​{1−cos⁡(π​t/T)}u_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2}\{1-\cos(\pi t/T)\} in its target SNR (42).

Tuning. We tune each forward process separately, because the shift acts differently on each. Per dataset, we train 1212 configurations of each graph-aware forward process, three shifts γ∈{10−3,3×10−3,10−2}\gamma\in\{10^{-3},3{\times}10^{-3},10^{-2}\} times four settings of its shape parameters, namely δ0\delta_{0} for MASS, α\alpha and cminc_{\min} for FCPS, and tct_{\mathrm{c}} for Cosine. The isotropic VP baseline has no shift and uses 1212 settings of scs_{\mathrm{c}} and tct_{\mathrm{c}}. We select the configuration with the lowest validation sliced Wasserstein distance (SWD) at 1010 DPM-Solver++2M steps, without using the graph metrics, and score it once on the test split. The grid stops at 10−210^{-2}, where the shift already moves λ1\lambda_{1} by 26%26\% and brings the forward process closer to the isotropic VP baseline. Both datasets have unit RMS per node, and we set σ\sigma to the RMS of the centered training signals, i.e., σ=1\sigma=1, except in the ablation.

Denoiser and evaluation. The denoiser is a time-conditioned ChebNet [73] with four residual blocks of Chebyshev order three and 6464 hidden units that predicts the clean signal. It trains for 4040 epochs, and we keep the checkpoint with the lowest validation denoising error. Within a dataset, all forward processes share the graph, the splits, the denoiser, its initialization, and the minibatch and noise draws of training. Our samplers step on a grid uniform in tt that stops at t0=10−3t_{0}=10^{-3}, where rt0r_{t_{0}} lies within 0.01%0.01\% of rmaxr_{\max}. The cosine ramp makes each step advance the log-SNR least at both ends of the horizon, where short steps reduce the discretization error [29]. We report mean and standard deviation over five paired seeds of initialization, training and sampling. In all tables, bold and underline mark the best and second-best methods, and a method evaluated at several numbers of reverse steps counts once, with its best entry. SWD compares 1,0241{,}024 generated with 1,0241{,}024 test signals, averaged over five draws of 128128 random projections.

Stiffness induced by the diffusion rate. The reverse-time stiffness LSL_{S} depends on the trained denoiser. To isolate the part that the diffusion rate creates, we set the frequency response of the denoiser to zero in the local stiffness (45),

LS(0)=supt,k|ζt,k||ht,k=0,L_{S}^{(0)}=\sup_{t,k}\left.|\zeta_{t,k}|\right|_{h_{t,k}=0}, (50)

which needs no training. We evaluate all diffusion rates on the same operator at each shift. At ht,k=0h_{t,k}=0, the theory gives LS(0),shared≥cT​λγ,maxL_{S}^{(0),\mathrm{shared}}\geq c_{T}\lambda_{\gamma,\max} and LS(0),MASS≤ML_{S}^{(0),\mathrm{MASS}}\leq M. For the cosine ramp, M=π2​log⁡(rmax/rmin)/TM=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\log(r_{\max}/r_{\min})/T, a factor π/2\pi/2 above that of the linear ramp, which keeps the logarithmic dependence on cond⁡(𝐋γ)\cond(\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}).

Table III confirms both bounds. Under the shared diffusion rates, LS(0)≈cT​λγ,maxL_{S}^{(0)}\approx c_{T}\lambda_{\gamma,\max}, and under MASS it lies within 3%3\% below MM, which makes MASS between 490490 and 1.5×1051.5{\times}10^{5} times less stiff. Over the tenfold range of cond⁡(𝐋γ)\cond(\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}), the stiffness of the shared diffusion rates grows tenfold, whereas that of MASS grows by at most 15%15\%, since it depends on the shift only through the span rmax/rminr_{\max}/r_{\min}. Fig. 1 shows the attenuation and the SNR behind this reduction. Under Cosine, the four highest graph frequencies are lost within the first tenth of the horizon, whereas the lowest keeps at,k>0.8a_{t,k}>0.8 beyond its middle, and the informative band of Proposition 3 shifts from high to low graph frequencies. Under MASS, all eight graph frequencies decay in the middle of the horizon, and every graph frequency follows the common target SNR rtr_{t}.

Sampling at a fixed number of reverse steps. We compare sample quality at fixed step counts using DPM-Solver++2M and DDIM, which solve the probability-flow ODE. At the selection point of Table IV(a), 1010 steps of the second-order DPM-Solver++2M [55], MASS improves on the best baseline by 17.9%17.9\% and 12.3%12.3\%, and beats every baseline in all five seeds on the stationary data and in at least four of five on the block-covariance data. Panel (b) tests whether a better solver can replace a better forward process, by comparing MASS with FCPS, the strongest graph-aware baseline, at 2525 steps of the first-order DDIM [52] and of DPM-Solver++2M. MASS remains best under both solvers, and under DDIM the SWD of FCPS is 1.471.47 and 1.081.08 times that of MASS. Forward-process design and fast solvers are therefore complementary.

Generation quality across graph frequencies. The spectral imbalance affects how the energy of a sample is distributed over the graph frequencies. We measure this on the samples of Table IV(a) with four errors against the test signals. The covariance error is the relative Frobenius error of the node covariance, the power-spectrum error is the relative ℓ1\ell_{1} error of the frequency-wise power 𝔼⁡[x~k2]\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}_{k}^{2}], the band-ratio error is the ℓ1\ell_{1} distance between the mean energy fractions of the lowest, middle and highest third of the graph frequencies, and the smoothness error is the Wasserstein-1 distance between the distributions of 𝐱𝖳​𝐋𝐱\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}. In Table V, MASS attains the lowest mean on every error except the smoothness error on the block-covariance data, where the isotropic VP baseline is lower with a spread that covers MASS. On the stationary data, MASS lowers the power-spectrum, band-ratio and smoothness errors of Cosine by factors of 1010, 5050 and 1515.

Fig. 2 compares the frequency-wise power of MASS with that of the isotropic VP baseline, the strongest baseline. On the stationary data, the isotropic VP baseline overshoots the upper half of the graph frequencies by about 15%15\%, whereas MASS stays within 8%8\% of the target everywhere. On the block-covariance data, MASS recovers the dominant GFT coefficient at λ0=0\lambda_{0}=0 within 9%9\%, whereas the isotropic VP baseline recovers only half of it and overshoots the next two graph frequencies by factors of 88 and 3.53.5.

Ablation of the forward-process parameters. MASS sets the target SNR and leaves two forward-process parameters free, the shift γ\gamma and the noise scale σ\sigma. Table VI varies one at a time on the stationary data around the selected MASS setting. Every row recalibrates the endpoints from the same tolerances, so that every row satisfies the same attenuation tolerances at both ends of the horizon.

On these data, gmin=γ​p0/σ2g_{\min}=\gamma p_{0}/\sigma^{2} is attained at λ0=0\lambda_{0}=0, so the span rmax/rminr_{\max}/r_{\min} grows in proportion to cond⁡(𝐋γ)\cond(\mathbf{L}_{\gamma}). By its definition, MM then grows by approximately π2​T​log⁡33\tfrac{\pi}{2T}\log 33, i.e., 5.55.5, over the upper block, which the table matches, whereas a shared diffusion rate would grow by a factor of 3333. SWD worsens by about 12%12\% at the two smallest shifts and is flat from γ=3×10−3\gamma=3{\times}10^{-3} on, so a larger shift improves MASS only marginally, while it moves every nonconstant eigenvalue by up to γ/λ1\gamma/\lambda_{1}, i.e., 7.7%7.7\% at 3×10−33{\times}10^{-3} and 25.7%25.7\% at 10−210^{-2}.

The noise scale leaves the attenuation unchanged by construction. Both gkg_{k} and the recalibrated endpoints scale as σ−2\sigma^{-2}, so at,k2a_{t,k}^{2}, MM and LS(0)L_{S}^{(0)} do not depend on σ\sigma, as the lower block shows. Only the noise level at which the denoiser trains changes, and the metrics move with it by about one standard deviation and without a monotone trend, which supports setting σ\sigma without tuning.

VI-B Downstream Tasks

We replace the isotropic forward process of three diffusion pipelines, for collaborative recommendation, traffic imputation and probabilistic spatio-temporal forecasting, with the MASS attenuation and noise variance (40). We keep their denoiser, conditioning variables, data splits and evaluation code, apart from the task-specific changes described below. To separate the graph operator from the diffusion rate, we also run the shared FCPS diffusion rate [25] on the same graph, denoiser and sampler, with its endpoints matched to the MASS attenuations. We call the two variants GAD-MASS and GAD-FCPS. Baselines are as reported in the original works, and the GAD rows report mean±\pmstd over five seeds.

Collaborative recommendation. We follow the collaborative filtering setup of CDiff4Rec [15]. The history of a user is a binary vector 𝐱0∈{0,1}n\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\{0,1\}^{n} over nn items, and the task is to rank the items absent from the history so that the held-out interactions appear at the top. CDiff4Rec corrupts the history with isotropic noise and recovers it with an MLP aided by the collaborative signals of similar users and review words, which it applies at 5050 diffusion levels. We view the history as a graph signal on an item graph that connects each item to the items with the most similar review profiles, so that the low graph frequencies are preferences shared by such items. We estimate pkp_{k} from the training histories, apply the denoiser once, at the rmaxr_{\max} end of the target SNR where at0,k2≈1a_{t_{0},k}^{2}\approx 1, and place 70%70\% of the training-time mass of πtr\pi_{\mathrm{tr}} on the four least corrupted levels to match. Both methods rank the items by the output of the trained denoiser, and we select one checkpoint per seed on validation Recall@20.

Table VII reports Recall@20 and NDCG@20, averaged over the test users. Recall@20 is the fraction of the held-out items among the 2020 top-ranked items, and NDCG@20 also weights each hit by the inverse of log2⁡(1+rank)\log_{2}(1+\text{rank}), normalized so that a perfect ranking scores 11. GAD-MASS improves on CDiff4Rec on every dataset and metric, by 5%5\% to 19%19\%, with one denoiser evaluation per user against 5050, whereas GAD-FCPS lies within −4%-4\% to +3%+3\% of CDiff4Rec.

Traffic imputation. We follow the traffic imputation setting of FENCE [12] on PEMS04 and PEMS08, where 307307 and 170170 road sensors record traffic flow every five minutes, with its spatially clustered, temporally contiguous (SC–TC) pattern. This pattern hides communities of neighboring sensors together for one hour with probability 0.80.8, so the hidden values must be inferred through the graph from sensors outside the community, and the imputation relies on the learned prior over graph signals. FENCE corrupts the readings with isotropic noise, trains an attention denoiser unconditionally and then conditioned on the observed entries, and samples with 5050 reverse steps under a guidance scale set per sensor cluster by a feedback rule. We view each time slice as a graph signal on the sensors. Since the reverse process regenerates only the hidden entries, pkp_{k} blends the clean power with the residual power left on them by the mean over neighboring sensors and time. We evaluate the feedback rule in the graph Fourier basis, where the reverse-step covariance of MASS is diagonal, keep the denoiser, masks and evaluator of FENCE, and add a fine-tuning stage at small numbers of reverse steps. We sample with Euler–Maruyama at 1616 and 2525 steps, take the median of ten samples as the imputation, and select checkpoints on validation at the same step count.

Table VIII reports the mean absolute error (MAE), the root mean squared error (RMSE) and the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE, as a fraction) on the hidden test entries. On PEMS08, GAD-MASS improves all three metrics at 1616 steps and further at 2525, where MAE, RMSE and MAPE fall by 6.8%6.8\%, 7.8%7.8\% and 10.9%10.9\%. On PEMS04, it matches FENCE in RMSE and MAPE at 2525 steps and trails it in MAE by 1.9%1.9\%, with half the reverse steps. GAD-FCPS gives two to four times the MAE of GAD-MASS at both step counts, worse than every baseline. This is consistent with Section V-B, since the largest reverse-time gain under a shared diffusion rate, attained at the highest graph frequency, may not be resolved at these step counts, whereas under MASS it does not grow with λγ,k\lambda_{\gamma,k}.

Probabilistic forecasting. We follow DiffSTG [13] on PEMS08, where the task is to forecast the next 1212 traffic slices of 170170 road sensors from the past 1212, with their uncertainty. DiffSTG masks the horizon in a window of history and horizon, corrupts the window with isotropic noise, trains UGNet to predict the noise, and samples eight trajectories with 100100 DDIM steps. Their mean is scored by MAE and RMSE, and the ensemble by the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), which rewards samples that are close to the reading and correctly spread. We view each time slice as a graph signal on the road graph of DiffSTG. Since the reverse process must generate what the history leaves undetermined, pkp_{k} is the residual power at λk\lambda_{k} after a per-frequency ridge regression of the horizon on the history, fitted on the training split. Three further changes go beyond the forward process. The denoiser predicts the clean horizon in the graph Fourier basis, its time embedding takes the attenuation and the noise variance as input, and the history slices follow their own forward trajectory during sampling.

We sample with DDIM in the graph Fourier basis at 33 and 88 reverse steps, on a grid uniform in log⁡rt\log r_{t}, where MASS gives every step the same increment of log-SNR at every graph frequency, and select one checkpoint per seed on validation CRPS. Table IX reports the results. With 33 steps against 100100, GAD-MASS improves the MAE and RMSE of DiffSTG, and at 88 steps it stays within 1%1\% of them. It trails DiffSTG on CRPS by 8.5%8.5\% and 4.5%4.5\% at 33 and 88 steps, and lowers the CRPS of GAD-FCPS by 88 to 9%9\%. The ensemble mean is accurate, but its spread is too narrow, and finer grids beyond 88 steps do not close the gap. A likely cause is that one clean power per graph frequency serves all twelve horizon steps, whereas the uncertainty grows with the step.

VII Conclusion

We have proposed and analyzed GAD, a graph-aware diffusion scheme that operates in the graph Fourier domain. The heat drift contracts each graph frequency at a rate proportional to its eigenvalue. With a shared diffusion rate, the resulting SNR imbalance affects denoising and can make the reverse SDE stiff. In our experiments, forward processes with a shared rate give no consistent gain over isotropic ones on the same graph and denoiser. MASS uses frequency-dependent diffusion rates to place all graph frequencies on one target SNR while keeping the GMRF prior. The analysis is exact for linear denoisers under graph stationarity, and MASS requires the eigendecomposition of the Laplacian and an estimate of the power spectrum of the data. Natural next steps are polynomial approximations for large graphs, clean powers that vary along the forecast horizon, and directed or time-varying graphs.
